Run rollback-only fresh SQL first with `node supabase/tests/run-pending-holds.mjs`; that command does not deploy the migration or establish browser acceptance.
- `reviewed-balances.gated.spec.ts` requires migration `202610060001`; it covers explicit timestamp/date-only posted activity review, conservative unconfirmed balances, later postings and retained undo history. A rollback-only migration test cannot enable this browser gate.
- `review-freshness.gated.spec.ts` asserts current→stale→unknown evidence, retained full saved review after a dated correction; denied scopes supply no balance data.
- `two-user-isolation.gated.spec.ts` exercises owned and foreign pages/APIs/files/RPCs/workflows, account/view histories and deterministic insight dismissal/restore/muting/exact relevance settings. SQL fixtures cover every current table and service boundary.
- `auth-refresh.gated.spec.ts` verifies persistent authenticated cookies; when supplied an actually expired session it also asserts rotation. Fresh-session acceptance alone does not prove rotation.
- `accessibility.gated.spec.ts` checks seven routes at360px, persisted dark appearance, native modal keyboard/background focus blocking/Escape/focus return. Scenario acceptance adds skip-link/de-DE/invalid horizon checks. These targeted checks are not a blanket WCAG certification.
- `import-control.gated.spec.ts` requires051 and exercises real partial Stop/Resume, worker fencing, exact progress/idempotency/source retention and full undo. Separate SQL/three-connection checks cover races; missing required migration fails explicitly.

Final acceptance also requires unit tests (enable live DB resolver parity), lint/build, fresh/upgraded schema checks and deployed revision/health/auth/journey checks. Production Vercel administration/cron/logs require actual project access; local success does not establish deployment success.

--- title: Ensuring instant navigations description: Learn how to structure your app to prefetch and prerender more content, providing instant page loads and client navigations. nav_title: Instant navigation related: title: Learn more description: Explore the full instant API, caching, and revalidation. links: - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/instant - app/guides/optimizing-prefetching - app/getting-started/caching - app/getting-started/revalidating - app/guides/prefetching --- This guide walks through understanding instant navigations, writing a route that navigates instantly, visualizing what's in the initial UI, and locking the behavior in with end-to-end tests. ## What "instant" means A navigation is **instant** when the browser can start rendering the new page the moment the user clicks, with static, cached, and fallback content showing up right away, while the server streams the remaining content into its fallbacks. > **Good to know:** This definition assumes caches are warm. Cold caches still require the server to compute the cached result once, so the first navigation to a route may still wait. A direct visit and a client navigation to the same route can produce different initial UI. **Direct visits** get the [**static shell**](/docs/app/glossary#static-shell) as HTML, typically from a CDN. **Client navigations** only re-render below the layout the current and destination routes share, so the fallback UI defined by a `` boundary above that point can't be used during the transition. Whether the new page appears instantly depends on the `` boundaries and caching present below the shared layout.
Why page loads and client navigations produce different initial UI On a page load, the entire page renders from the document root. Every component runs on the server, and anything that suspends is caught by the nearest `` boundary in the full tree. On a client navigation between `/store/shoes` and `/store/hats`, only the components below the `/store` layout re-render. A `` boundary in the root layout covers everything on a page load, but on this navigation, it sits above the re-render scope and does not trigger. content.thinking:
I'm thinking of a shared helper that fetches all pages by first requesting with an exact count so the total is known, then firing the remaining page requests concurrently rather than sequentially or speculatively. I need to watch out for consistency issues between the count and the actual paginated results if data changes mid-fetch.

Since supabase-js ties the count option to select() rather than letting me attach it afterward, I'm considering a simpler approach: fetch the first page, and if it's full, speculatively fire off the next few pages in parallel batches (say 4 at a time) without needing an upfront count at all — this cuts round trips significantly for both small and large result sets while keeping the helper's builder-function signature unchanged.

But I realize I need to check whether postgrest-js builders are safe to reuse across parallel `.range()` calls, since `range()` mutates the same URL object — if `.then()` triggers the fetch synchronously at call time, sequential reuse works, but parallel calls on one builder could race and overwrite each other's offset/limit before the fetch fires. The safer bet is a factory that creates a fresh builder per page, though I want to hold off deciding until I see the actual fetch timing data.

content.thinking:
I'm looking at the Home page's fetch waterfall: 55 fetches taking 1.86s total, with the transactions endpoint doing sequential pagination across five pages of 500 that account for roughly 1.2s of that time. The HomeHistory and AgentBriefing components appear to start fetching afterward, likely gated behind Suspense boundaries.

Since these Suspense children only start rendering after the main Promise.all resolves, they're effectively delayed behind the sequential pagination rather than streaming in parallel. I'm also noting the auth flow does getClaims then getUser plus workspaces in parallel adding ~130ms, and wondering whether getUser's network call could be skipped if getClaims can verify the JWT locally -- though that depends on whether the project uses asymmetric keys, since symmetric HS256 secrets force a fallback to the network call, raising security tradeoffs if removed.

My key fixes: first, parallelize the pagination in loadBalanceEvidence and similar helpers to save roughly 800ms, and bump the page size toward PostgREST's max_rows limit of 1000 combined with concurrent fetching. Second, since CashFlowPanel already has all six months of data loaded, I should move the In/Out/month selection to client-side state using the native history API to update the URL, making those interactions instant instead of triggering a full 1.9s server re-render with 55 fetches.

Now I'm working out how to keep MonthCashFlow's linked rows in sync with this client-side state — both need to read useSearchParams so the rows can call history.replaceState and scroll into view rather than triggering server navigation, while the server page still reads searchParams correctly on a hard load without re-rendering when the URL changes via replaceState.

For the trend chart, I should swap its router.replace call for history.replaceState too, avoiding an unnecessary server roundtrip.

Looking at the transactions page, I'm tracing the 13 fetches and ~600ms server time — auth, layout lookups, the transactions query, and editing history — and realizing the main ledger query could run in parallel with the account/category/view lookups instead of waiting on them, since it only depends on viewRow when a view filter is set, which could save 100-300ms; I'm also confirming root layout doesn't re-render on client navigation.

On prefetching, Next only prefetches up to the loading boundary for dynamic routes, which is fine since there's a root loading.tsx for instant skeletons, but adding staleTimes.dynamic for faster back-nav risks showing stale data after mutations that go through API routes rather than server actions, so I'll hold off until I measure. For the home page, I'm noting that independent Suspense sections like RecentTransactions, HomeHistory, AgentBriefing, and IouReview don't start their queries until after the main Promise.all resolves, which is delaying them unnecessarily.

The fix would be to kick off their loads earlier using cached loaders similar to what was done for insights and spending, and I also want to check the sequential delay in loadInsightEvidence between the transactions and effective_transactions queries. I'll wait for the benchmark to finish before digging further.

The server render makes 55 sequential Supabase calls (~1.86s), with `loadBalanceEvidence` paging through `transactions` 500 rows at a time as the main bottleneck—5 round trips taking ~1.2s that block every streamed section. Now checking the benchmark.

I realize a mutable shared builder would be unsafe for parallel use since retries are async, so I should use factories instead. I'm designing a shared pagination helper that reads all rows of an id-ordered query, using the first page's count and loading the rest in subsequent pages.

Rather than depending on count (which needs special select syntax), speculative parallel batching is simpler: fetch batches of pages concurrently and stop once a page returns fewer rows than requested, which safely signals the end without needing an exact count. I need to keep each caller's existing page size unchanged, since if the actual max_rows limit is smaller than my chosen page size, the loop could stop early and silently lose data — the `data.length < size` check is the safeguard against that.

Actually, I think I found the real issue: page.tsx builds `search` from account, month, and flow only — `show` isn't passed at all, meaning the Show toggle can never register as active since `search.show` is always undefined. For the benchmark's ready condition, I should drop the aria-pressed check and instead rely on the URL containing flow=out plus the presence of the h3 heading, since there are no h3s before the click. For the "Both" interaction check, I want to replace the current approach with something that actually waits for the server-rendered content rather than just the URL changing.

Since clicking canvas bars in echarts is hard to automate, it's simpler to swap out the "Both" interaction for toggling between Out and In via the Show control — starting at flow=out&show=out, clicking In, then waiting for the "Income by category" heading to appear. I'll patch the bench accordingly: strip the aria-pressed requirement from the ready condition, swap the Both interaction for this Out→In switch, and wrap each workflow step and interaction in try/catch for safety.

I spotted a pre-existing bug: the Show In/Out toggle doesn't filter bars since `app/page.tsx` never passes `show` to `CashFlowPanel`. I'll fix this as part of the cash-flow rework, and have the baseline harness wait for the breakdown to appear rather than checking the pressed state.

content.thinking:
I'm rethinking the client-side cash-flow selection design: having CashFlowPanel on the server load the data, then pass serialized view data into a new client component, CashFlowView, which manages selection state itself using the URL search params instead of relying on the current page.tsx-driven approach.

To keep the payload small and the client simple, I'm planning to pre-format everything server-side—month labels, amounts, percentages, hrefs for each of the four lists per month—so the client avoids reimplementing formatting logic.

For the "In"/"Out" links in MonthCashFlow, I'm considering a small FlowLink client component that intercepts clicks to update the URL via history state and scroll the cash-flow section into view, while still rendering a real anchor tag for accessibility and no-JS fallback. I'm weighing whether to use pushState or replaceState here, consistent with how TrendChart currently uses router.replace.

Deciding to use pushState for the link-based navigation (matching normal Link back-button behavior) and replaceState for the chart click, keeping consistency with the existing pattern. I'm confirming that Next.js integrates native pushState/replaceState calls with its router so usePathname and useSearchParams stay in sync, which means these client components can read params without needing page.tsx to pass them down—except for the account param, which HomeLiquidity still needs server-side.

I'm also checking that router.refresh and server action revalidation still work correctly with pushState-tracked URLs, and that useSearchParams doesn't require a Suspense boundary here since the page is dynamic. Now I want to look at the existing home-sections tests to see what contract they verify—likely rendering CashFlowPanel and checking links/aria-pressed—so I can update them accordingly.

I've found that every In/Out/Both and bar click triggers a full server re-render (~55 Supabase calls) despite `loadHomeSpending` already returning all six months' breakdowns. I'm now checking Next 16 docs on native history integration and the existing tests to design the fix.

content.thinking:
The real bug is isolated to page.tsx not passing the show param through, since the server component already supports it. I'm planning a minimal fix: add a client component that reads search params and renders links preserving the show state.

For click handling, I'll intercept plain left-clicks, push the new URL via history, and scroll the cash-flow panel into view using `scrollIntoView({block: "nearest"})` so it's a no-op when already visible but jumps to it from the MonthCashFlow rows.

For the server/client split, option B is cleaner: since React Flight supports bigint and Map serialization, I can keep CashFlowPanel as a server component that loads the raw data, then pass it down to a client component (CashFlowBreakdown) that reads search params and renders the TrendChart, legend, and TopLists itself—moving all the interactive pieces client-side while the server just fetches and forwards data.

I'm thinking AskAbout could be passed in as a ReactNode prop so the client component controls the full header layout alongside the legend. For testing though, this creates a wrinkle: since the client view will call useSearchParams() instead of taking a search prop, existing snapshot-style tests that render CashFlowPanel with a search argument will need to mock next/navigation's useSearchParams instead.

I'm also realizing MonthCashFlow's row links need rethinking — rather than computing the href server-side from search params, I should have CashFlowLink take a `changes` prop and compute its own href client-side using the current useSearchParams, which keeps SSR and client output consistent and should match existing test expectations like the anchor hrefs with month/flow query params.

For TrendChart's onSelect, I'll swap router.replace for history.replaceState directly since it's now a client view that can read params from useSearchParams. I'm also thinking through how Next's router patches pushState/popstate — since Next adds its own state marker, back/forward navigation through our pushState entries should still integrate with Next's internal tree restoration without triggering an unwanted refetch, since the underlying route tree stays the same.

The `account` param stays unchanged since HomeLiquidity handles it server-side via Links. Now I'm planning the new client component file for the cash flow view, moving TopList, legend, flowHref, and the chart wrapper into it, while keeping TrendChart as its own client component with the modified history.replaceState behavior. Then CashFlowPanel becomes a server component that loads data and passes it down to the new client view, including currency, locale, and an AskAbout element as a prop.

For serialization, I'm figuring out how to pass data that includes bigint fields and name mappings — React 19's Flight protocol handles Maps and BigInts fine, but I'll likely use plain Record objects for names instead of Maps for simplicity. I want to pass trend data (months, labels, income/spending numbers) and month-level grouped data with bigint fields, then format money and percentages on the client side rather than pre-formatting on the server, assuming format.ts is safe to use client-side.

I'll move the In/Out/month selection into a client component using `useSearchParams()` with `history.pushState`/`replaceState`, keeping data loading on the server since Next 16 syncs this without round trips. Now checking that the formatting helpers are client-safe.

The LLM call is cached per finding set via unstable_cache, so on a cache miss the Suspense section waits several seconds for the LLM, though it doesn't block other content since it's isolated in Suspense. Since my "ready" check waits for all aria-busy indicators to clear, a cache miss would delay the Overview's readiness, but since the seeded benchmark data is deterministic, findings should stay stable across runs and typically hit the cache, which persists in .next/cache.

Moving on, I should consider the router's staleTimes setting, which makes revisiting a page within 30 seconds feel instant by reusing the client-side cache — but this creates risk if mutations happen outside server actions, since router.refresh() clears that cache entirely while background processes like imports or agent runs could update server data without triggering a refresh, leaving a revisited page showing stale data within that 30-second window.

Given this is a finance app, I'd lean toward skipping staleTimes due to that correctness risk. As for aggressive prefetching on main nav links, that's also risky since it would force full server renders for heavy pages like Home (55 queries) on every viewport hit — better to rely on default prefetch behavior, which only renders up to the loading boundary for an instant skeleton, since the root loading.tsx is shared below the root layout. I want to check whether there are additional nested layout.tsx or loading.tsx files beyond the root.

content.thinking:
Checking the transactions drawer flow next: clicking a row triggers a full page re-render with auth, lookups, ledger, and drawer, but with my parallelized ledger change that stays efficient, and the Suspense boundary handles the drawer fine. Group-by and filter changes also just re-render the page at roughly two round trips, which is acceptable. For overall client navigation, each request still needs the local claims check plus a workspace requirement round trip, followed by one or two more for the page queries.

Each round trip runs roughly 70-200ms depending on Supabase's region, which sets the floor without caching. I consider whether requireWorkspace could be cached across requests, but since getUser's network call and the workspace lookup run in parallel, skipping getUser would only save a marginal amount and isn't worth weakening the security guarantees it provides. Turning to the staleTimes decision, I think about the user's goal of instant-feeling navigation given that without client-side caching, each navigation costs 300-600ms of server time, so setting staleTimes.dynamic to 30 would let back-and-forth navigation reuse cached data.

The main risk is stale data after mutations that don't trigger a router cache invalidation — I'm checking Next's docs on whether server actions automatically purge the client router cache, since typically it requires explicit calls to revalidatePath, revalidateTag, or cookie mutations, or a manual router.refresh. I want to check whether the actions in this codebase actually call revalidatePath.

What's left serialized is the auth dependency (mostly unavoidable) and the slow first transactions page, which takes 350ms likely due to loading 500 rows with embedded transaction sources.

I'm considering avoiding the count-first dependency by firing speculative pages, or trying a larger page size — though that doesn't clearly help. A better approach might be running a lightweight count request in parallel with the first page fetch, so the remaining pages can launch as soon as the count resolves rather than waiting for the full first page to complete, cutting the critical path roughly in half.

Looking at the critical path timeline, the auth call and sequential transaction pages dominate, finishing around 1497ms. The insight and spending chains add their own dependent stages, so with count-parallelization on balance evidence I'd cut roughly 200ms off anything depending on it, at the cost of one extra lightweight request per call—likely worthwhile overall.

I'm weighing whether to gate the parallel-count behavior only for large tables versus applying it generally, since the extra request is near-free on PostgREST but still adds overhead for small tables. I decide to just implement it generally in `allPages`, firing the count request alongside the first page so remaining pages can start before that first page even resolves.

Still refining the parallel-fetch logic...

content.thinking:
I'm trying to figure out why there's a 300-400ms gap between the chart chunk loading and canvas render—since hydration only kicks in at DOMContentLoaded, that delay seems too long just for echarts initialization and a bar chart render, so I'm wondering if echarts-for-react is deferring render with a setTimeout or something similar.

I'm also questioning why the HTML stream end time fluctuates so much (669-1033ms)—likely tied to whichever Suspense boundary resolves slowest, maybe WeeklyBriefing. The bigger puzzle is whether hydration truly waits for the full stream to finish or if React's selective hydration lets individual Suspense boundaries hydrate as soon as their chunk arrives, independent of DCL—which would mean the chart chunk request timing lining up with htmlEnd is more about Next's bootstrap script execution order than a hard architectural dependency.

I decide not to chase this further since the real bottleneck is server-side (the insights/categories/merchants fetch chain finishing around 1400ms), and that's a separate, larger refactor with diminishing returns right now. I'll commit the chart change, rerun the e2e specs, clean the seed data, and write up the PR, treating the chart fix as a client-only improvement that doesn't need to be re-validated against the full server bench.

I found that the chart chunk only loads after the full HTML stream finishes, meaning it's bottlenecked by the slow insights chain rather than JS size—I'll note this as a remaining issue instead of reworking the insights pipeline now, and commit the chart change.

input.content:
## Summary

Overview, Plan, Investigations and Transactions now load 32–45% faster. Picking In/Out (or a month) in Overview's cash flow went from **~1.2–1.4 s to ~20 ms**, with no server request. The Overview → Cash flow → Out → Uncategorized workflow went from **3.7 s to 1.75 s** (−53%).

The time went to **round trips to Supabase made one after another**, not to slow queries or rendering:

1. Ledger-sized reads paged through rows **one 500-row request at a time**. Overview waited on 5 sequential `transactions` pages (~780 ms) before anything streamed.
2. **Every cash-flow In/Out/month click was a server navigation** that re-rendered all of Overview (51 Supabase reads), though Overview already loads every month's breakdown.
3. A few pages waited on independent reads in sequence, and Investigations read every transaction's labels twice.

## Changes

| Commit | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `allPages` helper | Extracted the existing count-then-parallel pattern from `source-coverage.ts` into `lib/all-pages.ts`: the first page carries an exact count, the remaining pages load up to 6 at a time, and reading continues while pages come back full, so rows added meanwhile aren't dropped. Page sizes and ordering are unchanged. Used for balance evidence (Overview, Plan, every forecast), Overview spending, Plan → Spending, insight evidence and Investigations. In isolation the 2k-row balance-evidence `transactions` read went from **780 ms to 263 ms** (median of 7). |
| Cash flow in the browser | Selection (`show`/`flow`/`month`) moved into a client component (`app/cash-flow-view.tsx`) that reads `useSearchParams()` and updates the URL with `history.pushState`/`replaceState`, which Next 16 syncs with the router. Links stay real `<a href>`s (modifier-click and no-JS still work); back/forward and reload restore the pick. **Also fixes an existing bug:** Overview never passed `?show=` to the panel, so the Show In/Out toggle never filtered bars or showed as pressed. |
| Transactions | Without a saved view, the ledger query no longer waits for the accounts/categories/merchants/views lookups. |
| Agents | Runs and their open-proposal counts load together. |
| Overview preloads | History, Agent team and IOU review reads are memoized per request and start with the page, like the insight/spending reads already did, instead of after Overview's main data. |
| Investigations | The page shares its entities read with `runInvestigation` (passed explicitly, not via a hidden cache, because the chat tools can change categories/merchants mid-request). The label read runs alongside the others, and paging uses `allPages`. |
| Trimmed echarts | Overview/Plan/Settings charts only draw bar/line/scatter, so they register just those plus grid/tooltip/legend/mark-line. Model-written answer charts may use any type, so they keep the full build. Overview JS: **539 → 396 KB** (−27%). |
| Tests | Unit test for `allPages` (order, concurrency cap, rows added mid-read, errors); cash-flow tests now drive the URL; new gated e2e `home-cash-flow.gated.spec.ts` checks selection makes **no non-prefetch RSC request** and survives back/reload. |

**Deliberately not done:** `staleTimes.dynamic` / full `prefetch` would make revisits instant, but data also changes outside server actions (background imports, bank sync, agent runs, chat writes) with no router-cache invalidation. That could show stale balances, so I left it off.

## Measurements

**Test conditions.** `next build` + `next start` (production) on Windows 11, Node 22, Chromium (Playwright) at 1440×900, no throttling except where noted. Hosted Supabase over the internet (≈50 ms DB RTT; PostgREST calls 60–350 ms). Signed-in QA user with a **2,081-transaction ledger** (I seeded 2,000 tagged rows for realistic volume and removed them afterwards). 1 warm-up pass, then **5 runs; medians shown**, with min/median/max for key rows. The same harness ran against `main` (`ebd13951`) and this branch. Timings are taken in-page (`performance.now()` + rAF), from click to "new `<main>` rendered with no `aria-busy` sections". A server-side `fetch` hook counted every Supabase call. Two other dev servers were running on the machine, so there is real jitter (single outliers of 2–8 s on untouched pages).

### Workflow: Overview → Cash flow → Out → Uncategorized

| Step | Before | After | Change | Supabase calls |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1. Open Overview (hard load, chart drawn) | 1,776 ms | 1,016 ms | −43% | 55 → 55 |
| 2. Scroll to Cash flow | 0 ms (anchor) | 0 ms | — | 0 |
| 3. Select **Out** (breakdown shown) | **1,404 ms** | **20 ms** | **−99%** | **51 → 0** |
| 4. Open **Uncategorized** (filtered ledger shown) | 340 ms | 337 ms | ~0% | 9 → 9 |
| **Total** | **3,732 ms** (3,179–3,867) | **1,754 ms** (1,254–1,872) | **−53%** | |

Same workflow with **In**: 3,150 ms → 1,462 ms (−54%). Select In: 1,211 → 16 ms. Overview: 1,560 → 915 ms. Uncategorized: 316 → 331 ms.

The time went to **round trips to Supabase made one after another**, not to slow queries or rendering:

1. Ledger-sized reads paged through rows **one 500-row request at a time**. Overview waited on 5 sequential `transactions` pages (~780 ms) before anything streamed.
2. **Every cash-flow In/Out/month click was a server navigation** that re-rendered all of Overview (51 Supabase reads), though Overview already loads every month's breakdown.
3. A few pages waited on independent reads in sequence, and Investigations read every transaction's labels twice.

## Changes

| Commit | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `allPages` helper | Extracted the existing count-then-parallel pattern from `source-coverage.ts` into `lib/all-pages.ts`: the first page carries an exact count, the remaining pages load up to 6 at a time, and reading continues while pages come back full, so rows added meanwhile aren't dropped. Page sizes and ordering are unchanged. Used for balance evidence (Overview, Plan, every forecast), Overview spending, Plan → Spending, insight evidence and Investigations. In isolation the 2k-row balance-evidence `transactions` read went from **780 ms to 263 ms** (median of 7). |
| Cash flow in the browser | Selection (`show`/`flow`/`month`) moved into a client component (`app/cash-flow-view.tsx`) that reads `useSearchParams()` and updates the URL with `history.pushState`/`replaceState`, which Next 16 syncs with the router. Links stay real `<a href>`s (modifier-click and no-JS still work); back/forward and reload restore the pick. **Also fixes an existing bug:** Overview never passed `?show=` to the panel, so the Show In/Out toggle never filtered bars or showed as pressed. |
| Transactions | Without a saved view, the ledger query no longer waits for the accounts/categories/merchants/views lookups. |
| Agents | Runs and their open-proposal counts load together. |
| Overview preloads | History, Agent team and IOU review reads are memoized per request and start with the page, like the insight/spending reads already did, instead of after Overview's main data. |
| Investigations | The page shares its entities read with `runInvestigation` (passed explicitly, not via a hidden cache, because the chat tools can change categories/merchants mid-request). The label read runs alongside the others, and paging uses `allPages`. |
| Trimmed echarts | Overview/Plan/Settings charts only draw bar/line/scatter, so they register just those plus grid/tooltip/legend/mark-line. Model-written answer charts may use any type, so they keep the full build. Overview JS: **539 → 396 KB** (−27%). |
| Tests | Unit test for `allPages` (order, concurrency cap, rows added mid-read, errors); cash-flow tests now drive the URL; new gated e2e `home-cash-flow.gated.spec.ts` checks selection makes **no non-prefetch RSC request** and survives back/reload. |

**Deliberately not done:** `staleTimes.dynamic` / full `prefetch` would make revisits instant, but data also changes outside server actions (background imports, bank sync, agent runs, chat writes) with no router-cache invalidation. That could show stale balances, so I left it off.

## Measurements

**Test conditions.** `next build` + `next start` (production) on Windows 11, Node 22, Chromium (Playwright) at 1440×900, no throttling except where noted. Hosted Supabase over the internet (≈50 ms DB RTT; PostgREST calls 60–350 ms). Signed-in QA user with a **2,081-transaction ledger** (I seeded 2,000 tagged rows for realistic volume and removed them afterwards). 1 warm-up pass, then **5 runs; medians shown**, with min/median/max for key rows. The same harness ran against `main` (`ebd13951`) and this branch. Timings are taken in-page (`performance.now()` + rAF), from click to "new `<main>` rendered with no `aria-busy` sections". A server-side `fetch` hook counted every Supabase call. Two other dev servers were running on the machine, so there is real jitter (single outliers of 2–8 s on untouched pages).

- **Migrations not applied to the shared DB:** `202610260001_own_accounts` and `202610260002_iou_proposals` are in the repo but not applied, so `/money/accounts` and the transaction drawer error on this database (React #441 / `PGRST205`). - **Overview's chart waits for the whole HTML stream.** The echarts chunk is requested only when the stream ends, so on fast networks the chart lands ~300–500 ms after the cash-flow data, gated by the slowest streamed section (the 3-stage insight evidence chain + cached briefing wording).

- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.text:
I opened PR #108 with the optimizations and a full before/after report: https://github.com/indkhan/Moneo/pull/108

The slowness came from database calls made one after another, not from slow queries or rendering. Picking In or Out on Overview also re-ran the whole page on the server (51 database calls) every time.

All timings are from a local production build against your Supabase, signed in as the QA user with about 2,000 transactions. I added 2,000 test transactions for realistic volume and removed them afterwards. Each number is the median of 5 runs, before and after.

| | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Overview → Cash flow → Out → Uncategorized** | **3,732 ms** | **1,754 ms** (−53%) |
| ↳ Open Overview | 1,776 ms | 1,016 ms |
| ↳ Select Out | 1,404 ms | 20 ms (0 server calls) |
| ↳ Open Uncategorized | 340 ms | 337 ms (no measurable change) |
| Same workflow with In | 3,150 ms | 1,462 ms (−54%) |
| Overview page load | 1,461 ms | 803 ms |
| Plan page load | 1,333 ms | 904 ms |
| Investigations page load | 1,179 ms | 798 ms |
| Transactions page load | 651 ms | 426 ms |
| Transactions: group by / filter | ~510–525 ms | ~330–345 ms |
| Overview JavaScript | 539 KB | 396 KB |

**What I changed:**
- **Parallel page reads:** large reads now fetch their pages several at a time instead of one after another. The main transactions read went from 780 ms to 263 ms on its own.
- **Cash-flow selection in the browser:** In, Out and month picks no longer go to the server; back, forward and reload still restore the pick. This also fixed an existing bug: the Show In/Out toggle never actually filtered the bars.
- **Fewer waits:** a few pages now run independent reads together, and Investigations was reading every transaction's labels twice.
- **Smaller charts bundle:** the app's own charts load a trimmed chart library. AI answer charts keep the full one.

**Testing:** all 1,006 unit tests pass (9 gated tests skipped), and lint, type-check and the production build are clean. I added a browser test for the cash-flow selection. It passes, along with 3 existing browser specs. Three other gated browser specs fail. I checked each, and none is caused by this branch:
- `dated-overview` fails the same way with `main`'s code; it looks out of date since your last commit.
- `investigation` passes every investigation check, then fails opening the transaction drawer (missing database tables, below).
- `saved-view-scope` fails in its own cleanup step.

**Things you should know:**
- **Two migrations aren't applied to the shared database:** `202610260001_own_accounts` and `202610260002_iou_proposals`. Because of that, `/money/accounts` and the transaction drawer error out. I couldn't measure them, and I didn't apply migrations to a shared database without asking.
- **No browser-side caching of pages.** Caching would make returning to a page instant, but data also changes in the background (imports, bank sync, agents), so it could show stale balances.
- **Not improved yet:**
  - Uncategorized is held up by the sign-in check (60–300 ms per request), which I kept for security.
  - Overview's chart waits for the slowest section to finish loading.
  - Recurring reads detected patterns one batch at a time on purpose, to keep them in date order.
- **Noisy timings:** two other dev servers were running, so some runs spiked to 2–8 s. A few untouched pages (`/plan/currency`, `/settings`) came out slower on median. The PR shows those numbers as they are, with min/max ranges.
- Interaction responsiveness and layout-shift metrics, phone-speed CPU, and deployed (Vercel) speed weren't measured.

The benchmark scripts and raw results are in `.qa/perf/`, which git ignores.

content.thinking:
With only 498 total transactions, DB execution itself is fast (0.4-2.6ms) — the real bottleneck is round-trip latency, not the database. Indexes would matter at scale when many users' data causes sequential scans to grow linearly, so to demonstrate this honestly I'd need a synthetic test with much larger seeded data rather than my current 2k rows.

I'm reasoning through how RLS interacts with sequential scans: since the ownership-check function isn't leakproof, Postgres evaluates that security policy on every row scanned before applying the user's filter, meaning hundreds of thousands of per-row function calls on a large seq scan — which gets expensive fast. With a workspace_id index, though, since UUID equality is leakproof, the index condition can still be pushed down safely, avoiding that per-row evaluation cost.

The industry-standard fix is wrapping the ownership check as a subquery so it gets evaluated once via a hashed subplan rather than per row, which is exactly Supabase's documented RLS performance pattern. I'm also confirming this change is semantically equivalent to the original policy, and since the workspaces table policy doesn't reference other tables, there's no recursion risk, so this is a relatively safe, low-risk migration to apply across all the affected policies.

Before committing to a full rewrite across roughly sixty tables, I want to measure the actual performance impact with a synthetic test in a rolled-back transaction, inserting a large batch of fake transactions to see how much the query planning differs — though setting up a fake workspace with valid foreign keys to another user is a bit tricky, so I'm considering just using the QA user's own workspace for this test instead.

For a single large tenant, all rows match the owner filter anyway, so a seq scan is unavoidable regardless of indexing — meaning the real benefit would show up in the many-tenants scenario, where I'd need to generate several fake workspaces and corresponding auth.users rows, all safely inside a transaction I plan to roll back so nothing actually persists.

This is worth doing since the ask was about industry-standard, cheap, high-leverage fixes. I'll add indexes on workspace_id for hot tables plus a composite index on workspace_id and posted_on for transactions, and measure whether rewriting RLS policies actually matters at scale before committing to that change. But I should also note that right now, most of the user-facing latency is really network round trips, and the biggest industry fix for that is just co-locating the app server and database region — which means checking the Vercel deployment config to make sure the function region matches the Supabase region.

Beyond region co-location, I'm thinking about reducing round trips by merging many small PostgREST calls (like Home's 55 calls) into a single RPC, layering in caching with tag invalidation and stale-while-revalidate behavior, prefetching on hover intent, optimistic UI, and streaming/PPR so the shell renders instantly. For what I can safely implement now: add the index/RLS migration, consider caching getUser (though that's a security tradeoff I should flag to the user), and add hover-intent prefetching on rail links with a short stale window to balance freshness against speed.

Working out the hover-prefetch mechanics, I need to figure out whether Next 16's router.prefetch does a full prefetch or just the loading boundary, how Link's prefetch prop interacts with viewport vs hover triggers, and what staleTimes.static should be set to so that hovering doesn't serve minutes-old balance data — leaning toward a short window like 30 seconds since server actions already invalidate the router cache on mutations, but I need to weigh that against the earlier concern about stale balances.

Since Next enforces a minimum static staleTime of 30 seconds, I can't tune it tighter than that, but the actual benefit — shaving 150-300ms off navigation by starting the server render on hover — is a well-established pattern used by tools like instant.page and Linear, so the tradeoff of occasional 30-second-stale data on hovered-but-delayed clicks seems worth it, and I'm thinking about whether there's a mitigation to apply on the actual click.

I'm now considering a concrete failure case: a user hovers Transactions, triggers an import that completes via a background workflow rather than a router refresh, then clicks within 30 seconds and sees stale data since nothing invalidates the prefetch cache in that path. I'm weighing whether to surface this and the auth-caching tradeoff to the user via a question now, or finish the safe database work first and raise both tradeoffs at the end of the turn.

Queries themselves run in 0.4–2.6 ms, so the 60–300 ms latency comes from network/API overhead, not the database—though seq scans and RLS will hurt as data grows. I'll run a synthetic scale test to confirm this, but first need your input on two speed-vs-freshness/security tradeoffs before implementing them.

I'm thinking about using Link's prefetch prop with a null default for viewport-based prefetching, then switching to true on hover/focus/touch to trigger a full prefetch, since changing the prop value should re-trigger prefetch behavior.

Since full prefetch cache defaults to 300s via staleTimes.static, I need to override that to 30 seconds (the minimum allowed) in the experimental config to match what I told the user, while leaving dynamic at 0 so visited pages still refetch — this slightly shortens caching for static pages like privacy/terms, but that's negligible.

I'm sketching a small IntentLink wrapper component that tracks hover/focus/touch state and flips the prefetch prop to true once intent is detected, while being careful to merge any existing event handlers passed through props rather than overwriting them.

To avoid triggering a flood of full-page prefetches when a user quickly sweeps the mouse across multiple rail items, I'll add a short delay (around 60ms, similar to instant.page's approach) before marking intent, using a timer that's cleared on pointer leave.

For the auth caching layer, I'm setting up a short-lived in-memory cache keyed by user and session ID so that recently confirmed sessions skip the Supabase Auth round trip for about a minute, while still catching sign-outs and revocations within that window — and I'm making sure to skip caching if the session ID claim isn't present in the JWT.

I also need to bound the cache's size to avoid unbounded growth, confirm that signing out in the same browser is immediately effective since cookies get cleared regardless, and check where else `auth.getUser` is called across the app to make sure I'm only changing the right place. Next I want to write a synthetic scale test to quantify the cost of RLS checks and indexing before deciding on the migration.

For the test, I'm planning to insert 200k transactions into another existing workspace inside a rolled-back transaction, so nothing gets committed and other sessions never see the rows — checking that the row locks involved (new rows plus FOR KEY SHARE on referenced accounts) are benign. Then I want to run EXPLAIN as that workspace's user on the ledger page query to see how the RLS qualifier ordering affects the scan plan over the larger row count.

Since the leakproof uuid equality check on workspace_id can be reordered or combined by the planner regardless of security-barrier ordering, I'll just measure the actual plan rather than reason about it theoretically. After that, still within the same rolled-back transaction, I want to add an index and swap in a rewritten policy that checks workspace ownership via a subquery against the workspaces table, then re-measure — keeping in mind that subquery itself is also RLS-filtered by its own owner policy, so the two policies compose consistently.

Service role bypass doesn't matter here. Time to write the scale test itself.

I'll configure Next's staleTimes to the 30-second minimum with a ~60ms hover delay to avoid unnecessary prefetches, then test the database indexes and RLS rewrite at scale by inserting 200k synthetic transactions into a test workspace inside a transaction that's always rolled back, timing queries before and after.

With 68 policies having complex checks, rewriting all of them is too risky. I'm looking for a cheaper alternative: since there's an index on workspace_id, the planner can apply that index condition first, limiting rows before the per-row RLS qual even runs.

That means the per-row evaluation only scales with the user's own data, not the entire multi-tenant dataset -- so indexes alone likely solve the scaling problem, and the remaining per-row cost on a user's own rows is a smaller concern worth measuring separately. I'll start with indexes first, benchmark at scale, then run a synthetic test simulating a large single user to decide whether policy rewrites are actually needed.

Since 68 policies rely on `owns_workspace` and rewriting them all is risky, I'll first test whether simply indexing `workspace_id` captures most of the performance gain by letting Postgres filter rows before the RLS check runs—verifying this in a rolled-back transaction.

The exact count query is still slow since RLS evaluates per row — about 15µs per row, so a user with 20k transactions pays roughly 300ms just for the `count: "exact"` calls, including things like the transactions page header count and the first page of allPages.

The actual fix is likely rewriting the policy so `workspace_id in (select ...)` gets evaluated once as an initplan rather than per row. I want to test this directly on the transactions table by altering the select policy to use a subquery form and measuring whether the count speeds up.

Then I need to figure out how to apply this across all 68 affected policies — probably by dynamically detecting and rewriting any policy whose qual references the owns_workspace function, replacing it with the uncorrelated subquery form that Postgres can cache as an initplan.

I should also check whether lib/schema.ts defines these RLS policies via pgPolicy, since if so I'd need to update those definitions too alongside the SQL migration, and check for any supabase tests asserting policy behavior. Before anything else, I want to measure the actual benefit of the policy rewrite on count and view performance in the scale test.

Indexes cut the first-page query from 313 ms to 1.2 ms at scale, but exact counts still take ~310 ms since RLS evaluates `owns_workspace()` per row. Now I'll test Supabase's recommended policy pattern that computes owned workspace ids once per query instead.

git add supabase/migrations/202610270001_workspace_read_performance.sql lib/schema.ts && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Index workspace reads and check RLS ownership once per query

Policies called owns_workspace(workspace_id) per row, and most tables had
no index leading with workspace_id, so owned reads scanned every
workspace's rows. Policies now test workspace_id against
owned_workspace_ids(), an uncorrelated subquery evaluated once per query;
the same owner rule, owns_workspace is kept for the RPCs. Measured in a
rolled-back test with 200k other-workspace and 20k own transactions: the
ledger page went from 326 ms to 0.5 ms, its exact count from 319 ms to
16 ms and Home's six-month spending read from 111 ms to 10.5 ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline | head -1
